slides.title:
The author expects 200000.
What is printed?

slides.verdict_sub: and it is a data race (undefined behaviour)
bullets: No braces: the loop body is **only** the `lock_guard` declaration.
The guard locks and unlocks 100000 times, protecting nothing.
`++counter` runs once per thread, **after** the loop, unlocked.

slides.tip: GCC warns with `-Wall` (-Wmisleading-indentation). Treat warnings as errors in concurrent code.
slides.takeaway: A lock protects exactly the scope of its guard object. Always check where that scope ends.

text.body: This is the classic store-buffering (Dekker) test. Slide 3 shows why one small change in memory order changes the answer.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: if only Thread 1 uses release/acquire and Thread 2 stays seq_cst, is "nothing" possible? Reply below.

slides.title:
Two threads, two flags.
Which outputs are possible?
slides.cta: Pick all that apply, then swipe ➜

bullets: Nothing printed would need both loads to read `false`.
Then each load comes before the other thread's store in the single seq_cst order.
With program order that forms a **cycle**. Impossible.
"T1 T2" is fine: `x.store, y.store, y.load, x.load`.
slides.cta: Now change it to release / acquire ➜

slides.title: Same code, weaker ordering
slides.takeaway: Store then load on two different variables (Dekker pattern) needs seq_cst. Release/acquire does not forbid it.

"We use only std::atomic, no mutex. So our code is lock-free."

Interviewers love this one. True or false?
Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: Most people pick A. The real answer changes how you talk about lock-free code in interviews.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up an interviewer would ask next: "Your lock-free push calls new every time. Is it still lock-free?" Drop your answer below.

slides.title: Our code uses only std::atomic and no mutex. Is it lock-free?
options: Not necessarily. A thread may still wait on another thread's state.

slides.verdict_sub: Lock-free is about who can stall whom, not which headers you include.
bullets: `while (flag.test_and_set()) {}` is a lock. Preempt the holder and everyone spins.
`new` / `malloc` inside a push can take allocator locks.
slides.cta: Why not A, B or D ➜

items: A: locks can be hand-rolled from atomics, or hidden in library calls.
B: every atomic can be lock-free and the algorithm can still wait.
D: weak vs strong CAS is about spurious failure, not progress.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "every failed CAS implies another thread's CAS succeeded, and no step waits on another thread's state."

Memory ordering is the C++ topic most engineers bluff through in interviews.

Here is the mental model, plus the 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it for your next interview. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The two questions every atomic answers
2. The three layers you must never mix
3. The happens-before chain to say out loud
4. Why "thread 1 ran first" proves nothing
5. The exact definition of a data race
6. Six myths, busted (slides 7-8)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: the producer uses a relaxed store and the consumer an acquire load. Is the data safely published? Answer below.

slides.lead: What interviewers are actually checking for, and the answers that fail.

slides.title: Every atomic operation answers two separate questions

cards.label: Atomicity
cards.text: Can threads touch *this variable* without races, torn values or lost updates?

cards.label: Ordering
cards.text: What does it guarantee about *other* memory around it?

slides.takeaway: Atomicity is always there, even with `relaxed`. The memory order only changes the ordering answer.

slides.title: Never mix these in one answer
rows: instruction selection, compiler reordering, compiler barriers
slides.takeaway: Answer at the C++ level first. Hardware is one possible implementation.

slides.lead: Execution order is not synchronization. Only a happens-before edge makes the later read safe.

slides.title: The standard's definition
slides.warn: Result: undefined behaviour for the whole program, not "a stale value".

items.myth: "Release flushes the store buffer. Acquire invalidates the cache."
items.truth: Possible hardware effects. The C++ guarantee is a synchronizes-with edge when the acquire reads the released value.
Acquire never waits. A load that runs first just reads the old value and synchronizes with nothing.
Relaxed is still fully atomic. It is exactly right for counters and flags that publish nothing.
It constrains which outcomes are allowed, not scheduling.

items.myth: "Any memory barrier makes the code correct."
items.truth: You need a matched pair: release side and acquire side, on the same atomic object.

items.myth: "volatile is fine for a flag between threads."
items.truth: volatile gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering. Use std::atomic.

slides.hero:
Atomic:
"this operation is safe."

Memory order:
"how it relates to everything else."
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.
